title: The weak and the strong (Romans 14–15:7)
hookLine: don't quarrel over food and days; welcome one another

cards: Thanksgiving dinner. One cousin is vegan now. An uncle keeps making jokes about it.
Someone won't eat before grace; someone else has already started. One sister wants the holiday at church, another at the football game. Nobody is doing anything evil.
But by dessert, three people aren't speaking. The church in Rome had its own version of this table. Some believers kept careful rules about food and holy days.
Others ate anything and treated every day alike. And they judged each other. Paul, near the end of his letter, sits down at that table.

teach.h: RECEIVE THE WEAK, NOT TO ARGUE.
teach.b: Paul starts, in the King James Bible: "Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations." Welcome them, but not to argue.

He calls one group weak, those whose conscience holds them to careful rules about food and days, and the other strong, those who feel free. Paul counts himself among the strong. But notice where he puts the weight.
The strong mustn't look down on the weak. The weak mustn't judge the strong. And whoever's freedom might trip up a brother or sister should be willing to set it aside.
"One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind."
Each one answers to God, not to the person across the table.

teach.h: NOT MEAT AND DRINK, BUT PEACE AND JOY.
teach.b: Paul zooms out: "For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost." The dinner matters less than the people at it.
He lands here: "Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God."
Receive in Greek is proslambanesthe, to take someone to yourself, to welcome them in. The model isn't tolerance through gritted teeth. It's the way Christ received us.
Christians still argue about what counts as a food-and-days question and what's more central, and churches draw that line in different places; some point to this passage to keep a wide table.
A week of Romans up close: super-conquering, Paul's grief, the olive tree, a living sacrifice, love without a mask, the debt of love. It all comes down to sitting at one table together.

how: Christians often turn to Romans 14 when churches disagree over food, holy days, alcohol or worship styles, and some congregations use Romans 15:7 as a motto for hospitality.

o: take someone in and welcome them as your own
agree with someone's views so you can get along
put up with someone you can't change

games.q: what's inside the table — tap the pairs.
p: kept careful rules on food and days

s: Paul says the weak should become strong and drop their rules
he says each should be fully persuaded in their own mind, and the strong should bear with the weak.
Paul counted himself among the strong
yet he put the weight on the strong not to trip up the weak.
Paul says food and days are the heart of the kingdom of God
"the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy."

games.q: you feel free to eat anything. a fellow believer at your table keeps careful food rules, and your eating troubles their conscience. what does Paul say?
o: eat it anyway: you're right, and they need to learn.
be willing to set your freedom aside for them.
games.why: Paul counts himself strong, but says don't let your freedom trip up a brother or sister: "receive ye one another, as Christ also received us."

practice: Picture someone who practices, eats, votes, worships or celebrates differently from you, in a way that sometimes gets under your skin, and notice any small judgment that rises, without feeding it.
Then imagine pulling out a chair for them at your table, not to fix them, just to welcome them, and meaning it. If you pray, pray for them by name, and for yourself.

wordCard.voice: Proslambanesthe. Paul's Greek word for receive: to take someone fully to yourself, the way Christ received us at the table.

orig.note: Greek: receive, welcome, take someone to yourself.

carryVoice: Your line: welcome one another. There's room for everyone at the table. See you tomorrow.
